analysis.one_liner: Taxes half the profits of major oil companies during gas price spikes and rebates the money to households.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced by a single House member with zero cosponsors, it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: During any quarter when average U.S. gas prices were as high as they were on the day Russia invaded Ukraine, major integrated oil companies would have paid a 50% excise tax on their profits, rising to 75% if the company raised pump prices in response. The money would go into a Gas Profit Recovery Fund and be paid out as quarterly tax rebates to households, phasing out for incomes above $100,000 ($200,000 for joint filers). The bill never advanced past its referral to the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Households paying high gas prices would receive quarterly refundable rebates funded entirely by the oil-company tax. The credit phases out at higher incomes, so the money tilts toward middle- and lower-income households, and joint filers would get 150% of the single-filer amount.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households hit by high gas prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill taxes 50% of the profits of major integrated oil companies in any quarter when national average gasoline prices meet or exceed their February 24, 2022 level, and the revenue is appropriated to a Gas Profit Recovery Fund to finance rebates.

The rebate is a refundable credit paid quarterly, with joint filers receiving 150% of the single-filer amount and the credit phasing out by 5% of adjusted gross income above $100,000 for single filers, $150,000 for heads of household, and $200,000 for joint returns.
The tax rate rises to 75% if the Treasury Secretary, consulting Energy and the FTC, finds a company raised prices in response to the tax, an explicit anti-pass-through provision.
The tax base adds back executive bonuses and stock buybacks, so companies could not shelter profit from the tax by paying executives or buying back shares.

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies (those meeting a lowered $500 million asset threshold for the 'major integrated' definition) would bear the excise tax through the end of 2023. Some of the cost could be passed to consumers at the pump, which the 75% penalty rate is designed to deter but cannot guarantee against.

drawbacks.text: Oil companies could pass some of the tax through to consumers in higher pump prices; the bill's answer — a 75% rate for companies found to have raised prices in response — depends on a determination by Treasury after consultation with Energy and the FTC and would be difficult to police in practice.

A temporary tax on oil profits can discourage new drilling and refining investment, which critics argue tightens supply and keeps prices higher over time; economists have long debated windfall-profit taxes on exactly these grounds.

The tax is short-lived, ending after December 31, 2023, so any relief for consumers would be temporary, and it applies only in quarters when average gas prices are already high — it does nothing to lower the price at the pump directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: money taken from oil-company profits in high-price quarters and handed to households as rebates. The pass-through risk is real but mitigated by design (the 75% penalty rate and the add-back of bonuses and buybacks), and the temporary window limits both the benefit and the investment-side cost. The bill's bigger weakness was political, not design: it attracted no cosponsors and no committee action, so it was never tested or improved.

outcome.mechanism: A single House member introduced it, the Ways and Means Committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-NY) introduced the Stop Profiting Off Putin's War Act on March 16, 2022, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill received zero cosponsors in the House.
No further action appears in the bill's history after the committee referral — no markup, no hearing, no floor vote — and the 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, killing the bill.
The Ways and Means Committee, which holds jurisdiction over excise taxes, took no action on the bill in the ten months it was pending.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies, which kept the windfall profits generated by the 2022 price spike rather than paying the 50% tax, and households never received the rebates the bill would have funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies kept windfall profits

for.name: Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; no other House member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for excise taxes
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill in the ten months after referral.

against.name: Major oil companies and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed windfall-profits-tax proposals advanced after the February 2022 price spike, arguing they would discourage investment and raise pump prices.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so the partisan shape of support was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would take 50% (or 75% in a pass-through finding) of these companies' profits in any high-gas-price quarter through 2023, a direct hit to the earnings they were realizing from the 2022 price spike. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the rebate households would have received.
Households would have received quarterly refundable rebates funded by the oil-company tax, phasing out above $100,000 of income for single filers.
